Part 2 - A Business Forecasting Horse Race: ARIMA vs. ETS

2.1a. The Data

pacman::p_load(tidyverse, fpp3, BVAR, feasts)

#Importing data set from file folder
liquor_raw <- read_csv("Data/MRTSSM4453USN.csv",
                       na = ".",
                       col_types = cols(
                         observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
                         MRTSSM4453USN = col_double()))

# Creating time series object indexed monthly and renaming columns
liquor <- liquor_raw |> 
  transmute(
    Month = yearmonth(observation_date),
    sales = MRTSSM4453USN
  ) |> 
  as_tsibble( index = Month) |> 
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2019 Dec") )

# checking for gaps in time series 
has_gaps(liquor)

2.1b. Plotting Sales

#graphing sales with autoplot
autoplot(liquor, sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly Retail Sales of liquor in the United States (Millions of Dollars)",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Sales (Millions of Dollars)")
#Graphing seasonal monthly sales by year with gg_season
gg_season(liquor, log(sales)) +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly Retail Sales of liquor in the United States (Log-Scale)",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Sales (Log-Scale)"
  )

The overall trend of liquor sales in the united states shows a seasonal monthly trend that is growing overtime. Seasonal swings look to grow with the level of the series. The difference between the peaks and troughs are greater in 2020 than in 2000, showing greater seasonality than previous subsequent years. November moving into December shows the fastest growth of liquor sales and is accompanied with the highest overall sales in a calendar year. The lowest liquor sales start in January and reach its peak in December. Using log scale shows a greater rate throughout the year.

2.2

2.2a.

#Fitting an ARIMA model and ETS model to the log of sales
liquor_fit <- liquor |> 
  model(arima = ARIMA(log(sales)),
        ets = ETS(log(sales)))

#Assessing specification of each model
liquor_fit |> select(arima) |>  report()
Series: sales 
Model: ARIMA(1,0,2)(2,1,1)[12] w/ drift 
Transformation: log(sales) 

Coefficients:
         ar1      ma1     ma2    sar1     sar2     sma1  constant
      0.8948  -0.7374  0.2477  0.3679  -0.2334  -0.8845    0.0036
s.e.  0.0355   0.0697  0.0623  0.0668   0.0665   0.0468    0.0001

sigma^2 estimated as 0.0005469:  log likelihood=752.43
AIC=-1488.85   AICc=-1488.4   BIC=-1458.61
liquor_fit |> select(ets) |> report()
Series: sales 
Model: ETS(A,A,A) 
Transformation: log(sales) 
  Smoothing parameters:
    alpha = 0.3296099 
    beta  = 0.007560263 
    gamma = 0.0001765132 

  Initial states:
     l[0]         b[0]      s[0]      s[-1]        s[-2]       s[-3]      s[-4]
 7.412219 0.0007608238 0.3263441 0.03153301 -0.004849389 -0.03530501 0.02512163
      s[-5]      s[-6]      s[-7]       s[-8]      s[-9]     s[-10]     s[-11]
 0.05558624 0.01219515 0.02503206 -0.06088935 -0.0607952 -0.1578065 -0.1561667

  sigma^2:  7e-04

      AIC      AICc       BIC 
-489.1517 -487.2272 -424.2608

The ARIMA model specification was (1,0,2)(2,1,1)[12] with drift. This means a non-seasonal single lag, no month-to-month differencing, and 2 lagged forecast errors. Then a seasonal lag of 12 and 24 months prior, a seasonal differencing which is this month minus the same month as last year, and 1 lagged forecast error. This was differenced by taking the value of a month and subtracting the value of the same month from the year prior. ETS specification was (A,A,A) which means the error, trend, and seasonality are all additive. This is due to taking the log of sales. The additive components correspond to multiplicative effects in dollars.

2.2b. ljung-box test

# Checking residuals of ARIMA model
liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> gg_tsresiduals()
#Ljung-Box test of residuals of ARIMA model
liquor_fit |> 
  select(arima) |> 
  augment() |> 
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24, dof = 6)
# A tibble: 1 × 3
  .model lb_stat lb_pvalue
  <chr>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 arima     120.         0

The ljung-box test returned a p-value of 0, which is less than 0.05 or 5% critical value. This means we reject the null hypothesis meaning there is statistically significant evidence that there is autocorrelation in the residuals and its not solely white noise.

The dates of the first and last forecast are January 2002 and December 2019. Using the MSE and MAE, the ARIMA model performs better then the ETS and SNAIVE. Without the Diebold-Mariano test, we cannot be 100% positive on how much better the models are to each other.

2.4

#creating tibble of forecast errors for each model
liquor_errs <- liquor_cv_fc |> 
  as_tibble() |> 
  left_join(as.tibble(liquor) |> select(Month, actual = sales),
            by = "Month") |> 
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |> 
  select(Month, .model, e) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e) 

#Diebold-Mariano test comparing ARIMA to ETS
dm_arima_ets <- forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets, h =1, power = 2)

#Diebold-Mariano test comparing ARIMA to SNAIVE
dm_arima_snaive <- forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$snaive, h = 1, power = 2)


dm_table <- data.frame(
  Comparison   = c("ARIMA vs. ETS", "ARIMA vs. SNAIVE"),
  DM_statistic = c(dm_arima_ets$statistic, dm_arima_snaive$statistic),
  p_value      = c(dm_arima_ets$p.value,   dm_arima_snaive$p.value)
)

knitr::kable(dm_table, digits = 3,
             col.names = c("Comparison", "DM Statistic", "p-value"),
             caption = "Diebold-Mariano Tests (squared-error loss, h = 1)")
Diebold-Mariano Tests (squared-error loss, h = 1)
Comparison DM Statistic p-value
ARIMA vs. ETS -2.906 0.004
ARIMA vs. SNAIVE -10.755 0.000

Using the Diebold_Mariano test, a p-value resulted in .004 and 0 explain that the there is statistically significant evidence to reject the null hypothesis. The accuracy between the test differ. Since the DM statistic is negative, this demonstrates that the ARIMA model is more accurate than both the ETS and SNAIVE model. The DM confirms what the previous table illustrated. If I was a business owner, I would use the ARIMA model over the ETS and Random Walk Model.

Part 3 Forecast Combination

3a

# Model Combination of ARIMA and ETS
liquor_combo_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |> 
  mutate(combo = (arima + ets) / 2 ) |> 
  forecast(h = 1)

#Testing accuracy of model combinations to their individual models
liquor_combo_fc |> 
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
.model .type RMSE MAE
arima Test 81.43 65.65
combo Test 85.19 66.77
ets Test 94.35 72.31
snaive Test 161.26 136.63

The combo model that balances between the ARIMA and ETS perform better than the ETS and SNAIVE models, however, the ARIMA model by itself performs better than the combination model.

3b

#Computing correlation of errors between ARIMA and ETS
cor(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets)
[1] 0.8782934

A correlation of .88 means the errors between the ARIMA models and ETS model are highly correlation. This high correlation is confirmation from the combination accuracy table because a combination of models with similar errors typically doesn’t outperform the individual models. In this case the combo performed better that ETS, but not ARIMA. The ARIMA model performs better than the ETS, so when combining it with the worse model it decreases the accuracy.

4.2

#Estimating VAR
var_ols_fc <- function(z,p) {
  e <-  embed(z,p +1)
  M <- ncol(z)
  B <- coef(lm(e[, 1:M] ~ e[, -(1:M)]))
  x <- c(1, t(z[nrow(z):(nrow(z) - p + 1), ]))
  x %*% B
}

fc_var1 <-  NULL
fc_var4 <- NULL
for (T in origins) {
  fc_var1 <- rbind(fc_var1, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ],1))
  fc_var4 <- rbind(fc_var4, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ],4))
}

#Computing RMSE of each model for each variable
rmse_by_var <- function(f) sqrt(colMeans((actual - f)^2))

rmse_by_var(fc_var1)
      gdp      cons        iv       emp      infl    unrate       ffr      gs10 
0.5130384 0.4598547 2.4927057 0.1956584 0.2084055 0.1988068 0.3902989 0.3610310 
rmse_by_var(fc_var4)
      gdp      cons        iv       emp      infl    unrate       ffr      gs10 
0.5693241 0.5268484 2.5212629 0.2277561 0.2069608 0.2153966 0.4973504 0.3789663

The Var(1) model forecasts better than the var(4) model for 7 of the 8 variables. The only variable where var(4) beats var(1) is in inflation and is only better marginally. Our data includes 240 observations from 1990 to 2019. The Var(4) includes more regressors than the var(1) in a small data frame. The var(4) is over fitting the data while the simplier model has more degrees of freedom to try and model.

4.3a

# Estimating BVAR(4) with a Minnesota Prior
bvar_cv <- function(lambda) {
  pr <- bv_priors(hyper = "lambda",
                  mn = bv_mn(lambda = bv_lambda(mode = lambda, sd = 0.4,
                                                min = 0.999 * lambda,
                                                max = 1.001 * lambda),
                             b = 0))
  fc <- NULL
for (T in origins) {
  fit_T <- bvar(y[1:T, ], lags = 4, priors = pr,
                n_draw = 2000, n_burn = 1000, verbose = FALSE)
  x <- c(1, t(y[T:(T - 3), ]))
  fc <- rbind(fc, x %*% coef(fit_T))
}
  fc
}

The BVAR(4) lambda(0.3) performs better than the VAR(4) even though they contain the same variables and lags. The BVAR’s shrinkage reduces the estimation noise by pulling the lags down closer to 0. I can confidently say BVAR(4) lambda(0.3) is better than VAR(4) because they share the same lag structure and data. The BVAR(4) lambda(0.3) outperforms the VAR(1) in 3 of the 8 variables. This is not as easy of a comparison between the BVAR(4) lambda(0.3) and the VAR(4) though. A Diebold-Mariano test will be needed in order to compare accuracy. When lambda is 0.05, the model is shrinking the lags too close to zero its and biasing the estimates in the other direction. Some of the variables are positively correlated with its lag, so with a tighter lambda, the model is trying to forecasts the variables the average. RMSE would not be a fair estimate, because I chose the model with the lowest RMSE using the same evaluation sample, the winner’s RMSE is likely optimistically biased: part of its advantage may reflect luck in this particular sample. A fair estimate would require evaluating the chosen model on a separate holdout period not used for model selection.

Part 5 - A Factor Model with FRED-MD

5.1a.

md_raw <- read_csv("data/fredmd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
tcode <- unlist(md_raw[1,-1])
md <- md_raw[-1, ] |> 
  mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y"))

#Transformation Code
transform_series <- function (x, code) {
  d <- function(v) c(NA, diff(v))
  switch(as.character(code),
         "1" = x,
         "2" = d(x),
         "3" = d(d(x)),
         "4" = log(x),
         "5" = 100 * d(log(x)),
         "6" = 100 * d(d(log(x))),
         "7" = d(x / dplyr::lag(x) -1))
}

5.1b.

#Applying transformations to each series
fm <- map2_dfc(md[names(tcode)], tcode, transform_series) |> 
  mutate(date = md$date, .before = 1) |> 
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

fm <- fm[, colSums(is.na(fm)) == 0]

dim(fm)
[1] 718 122

5.1c.

# Transformation codes for each series
tcode[c("INDPRO", "PAYEMS", "CPIAUCSL", "FEDFUNDS")]
  INDPRO   PAYEMS CPIAUCSL FEDFUNDS 
       5        5        6        2

INDPRO is the growth rate of total industrial production across the entire series. PAYEMS is also the growth rate of labor/employment for 80% of the labor force. CPIAUCSL is the change in the growth rate for the consumer price index. This tracks how inflation is changing for consumers when buying bundles. FEDFUNDS is the first differences, this shows the difference between or rate of change for the federal funds rate. Series need different transformations because of how they are measured. INDPRO is total production, so knowing the growth rate of industrial production can help predict future INDPRO becasue we know on average how it moves in the future. Compared to the FEDFUNDS which needs first differences because the fedfunds rate is measured by an increase or decrease from what it was from the previous time.

5.3

# Replicating Horse Race
ip <- fm$INDPRO
n <- nrow(Z)
init <- which(fm$date == as.Date("1989-12-01"))

e_ar <- NULL
e_fa <- NULL
for (T in init:(n -1)) {
  F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:3]
  d <- data.frame(y_next = ip[2:T], y = ip[1:(T-1)], F_T[1:(T-1),])
  new <- data.frame(y=ip[T], t(F_T[T, ]))
  e_ar <- c(e_ar, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~y,d),new))
  e_fa <- c(e_fa, ip[T +1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ ., d), new))
}

c(RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)))
  RMSE_AR   RMSE_FA 
0.6168431 0.5887272

Estimating the factors on the full sample would introduce look-ahead bias: the factor loadings and standardization would use data from after the forecast date, including the value being forecast. Re-estimating the factors at each origin using only data available at that time ensures a fair, real-time comparison with the AR(1).

5.4

direct_race <- function(series, h = 12, r = 3) {
  lv <- md |>
    mutate(log_x = log(.data[[series]]),
           g = 100 * (log_x - lag(log_x))) |>
    filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))
  yh <- 100 * (lead(lv$log_x, h) - lv$log_x)      
  g  <- lv$g                                     

  e_ar <- NULL
  e_fa <- NULL
  for (T in init:(n - h)) {
    F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:r, drop = FALSE]
    i <- 1:(T - h)
    d <- data.frame(yh = yh[i], g = g[i], F_T[i, , drop = FALSE])
    new <- data.frame(g = g[T], F_T[T, , drop = FALSE])
    e_ar <- c(e_ar, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ g, d), new))
    e_fa <- c(e_fa, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ ., d), new))
  }
  tibble(series, forecasts = length(e_ar),
         RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)),
         MAE_AR = mean(abs(e_ar)), MAE_FA = mean(abs(e_fa)),
         DM_pvalue = forecast::dm.test(e_ar, e_fa, h = h, power = 2,
                                     varestimator = "bartlett")$p.value)
}

direct_race("CPIAUCSL")
# A tibble: 1 × 7
  series   forecasts RMSE_AR RMSE_FA MAE_AR MAE_FA DM_pvalue
  <chr>        <int>   <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
1 CPIAUCSL       349    2.11    1.89   1.58   1.35  0.000443

Adding the first three factors reduces the RMSE of 12-month-ahead CPI inflation forecasts by about 10% (from 2.11 to 1.89) and the MAE by about 15%. The Diebold–Mariano test, adjusted for the autocorrelation in overlapping forecast errors, rejects equal predictive accuracy (p < 0.001), so the improvement is statistically significant.

Reflection

This problem set was a bigger task than the previous.
